```{r}
#| label: Libraries Setup
#| results: hide

#Load Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytuesdayR)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthdata)

```

Step one is to load all the necessary libraries.

```{r}
#| label: Dataset Check
#| results: hide

#let's use the cat dataset for this map
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load('2023-01-31') #create data object from tidy tuesday library

#extract the cat data
cats_uk <- tuesdata$cats_uk
cats_uk_reference <- tuesdata$cats_uk_reference

#data structure check
head(cats_uk)
head(cats_uk_reference)
```

My goal is to use the uk_cats dataset to project locations over the United Kingdom.

```{r}
#| label: Creating Basemap Object
#| fig-cap: Test Basemap Projection
#| results: hide

#create spatial object of the United Kingdom to project points over

uk_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", country = "United Kingdom", returnclass = "sf")

#visual check
ggplot(uk_map) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "white") +
  theme_void()

#structure check
st_crs(uk_map)
```

My first step is to make an sf object of the United Kingdom as a basemap. I do a quick visual check to make sure it projects correctly in ggplot. The result looks good. A structure check confirms the correct coordinate system.

```{r}
#| label: Points data as sf object
#| fig-cap: Test Point Map

#use st to sf function to create sf object of data points

cats_uk_sf <- st_as_sf(
  cats_uk, 
  coords = c("location_long", "location_lat"), 
  crs = 4326)

#visual overlay of points on basemap

ggplot(uk_map)+
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "white")+
  geom_sf(data = cats_uk_sf, color = "blue", size = 2, alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()
```

Next I want to take the coordinate data from the uk cats dataset and convert those observations into point data that I can project on my map. I use the st_as_sf function to turn the csv data into an sf object. I then project the data over my UK basemap to see if it looks good...

Wow! All of the cats live in Devon and Cornwall! I need to make my basemap smaller.

```{r}
#| label: Making a Smaller Basemap
#| fig-cap: Test County Map

#pull the county data as an sf object
uk_counties <- ne_states(country = "United Kingdom", returnclass = "sf")

#filter counties to just the two I want to make new basemap
devon_and_cornwall <- uk_counties |>
  filter(name %in% c("Devon","Cornwall"))


#test projection on my smaller sf basemap
ggplot(devon_and_cornwall)+
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "white")+
  geom_sf(data = cats_uk_sf, color = "blue", size = 2, alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()
```

Wow, all the cats actually just live in Cornwall. We could have avoided this by naming it cornwall_cats rather than uk_cats.

```{r}
#| label: Literally a basemap of Cornwall
#| fig-cap: Test Cornwall Map

literally_just_cornwall <- uk_counties |>
  filter(name == "Cornwall")

#test projection again on the map
ggplot(literally_just_cornwall)+
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "white")+
  geom_sf(data = cats_uk_sf, color = "blue", size = 2, alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()

```

Now let's make a nice pretty map with labels and a pleasing color scheme.

```{r}
#| label: A final map
#| fig-cap: Cats in Cornwall, Take 1
#| out-width: "125%"

#map with different colors for different cats, on a nice background
ggplot(literally_just_cornwall)+
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "black")+
  geom_sf(data = cats_uk_sf, aes(color = tag_id), size = 2, alpha = 0.7  )+labs(title = "The Wandering Cats of Cornwall",caption = "Data from tidytuesdayR package")+
  scale_color_discrete(type = "plasma",guide = "none")+
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 16,face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,face = "italic"))
  


```

This map is unfortunately a mess. With over 100 cats tagged in the dataset, it's impossible to get a color scale that shows each cat on the map. The resulting layout is highly confusing. To make something that is visually understandable, I am going to artificially condense the cats point dataset so it only filters the locations of eight individual cats.

```{r}
#| label: Creating a data subset for a more digestible map
#| fig-cap: Subset of Cornwall Cats

#use filter function on cat points data to select eight individual felines
just_eight_cats_from_cornwall <- cats_uk_sf |>
  filter(tag_id %in% c("Ares","Indie-Tag","Tigger-Tag","Balu-Tag","Coco","Alfie-Tag","Carrots-Tag","Friday"))

```

This code chunk above selects just eight kitties, much easier to visualize on a map display.

```{r}
#| label: A final map!
#| fig-cap: Cats in Cornwall revised
#| out-width: "125%"

#The same map as above with only the eight selected cats
ggplot(literally_just_cornwall)+
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgrey",
          color = "black")+
  geom_sf(data = just_eight_cats_from_cornwall, aes(color = tag_id), size = 2, alpha = 0.7  )+labs(title = "The Wandering Cats of Cornwall",
                              subtitle = "Map of Cornwall County,England",
                              caption = "Data from tidytuesdayR package")+
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo",name = "Cat Name",labels = c("Ares","Balu","Carrots","Coco","Friday","Alfie","Indie","Tigger"))+
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 16,face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,face = "italic"))
```

The final map has a discernible legend, and the color scheme has been changed so the cat points are more distinct. Realistically, this dataset would be best projected at a city or even neighborhood level. Even within a small county, it is difficult to get more than just a general sense of where the cats are located.

```{r}
#| label: saving output image as jpeg file

#use here function to save to output folder
ggsave(here("Week_07","Outputs","cornwall_cat_map.png"))

#save my edited dataframe as a csv as well
write.csv(just_eight_cats_from_cornwall,file=here("Week_07","Outputs","cornwall_cats_subset.csv"))
```

Finally I will save my outputs to the correct folder for uploading to GitHub.
